## Phonology

### Consonants

| | Bilabial | Labiodental | Dental | Alveolar | Post-alveolar | Palatal | Labial-velar | Velar | Glottal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nasal** | m |  |  | n |  | ɲ |  |  |  |
| **Plosive** | p · b |  |  | t · d |  | c |  | k · ɡ | ʔ |
| **Affricate** |  |  |  |  | dʒ |  |  |  |  |
| **Sibilant fricative** |  |  | s̪ | s | ʃ |  |  |  |  |
| **Non-sibilant fricative** |  | f |  |  |  |  |  |  | h |
| **Approximant** |  |  |  |  |  | j | w |  |  |
| **Lateral approximant** |  |  |  | l |  |  |  |  |  |
| **Trill** |  |  |  | r |  |  |  |  |  |

Where symbols share a cell, the voiceless ones come first and the voiced follow the dot. Secondary articulation (ʷ ʲ ˠ ˤ) and length (ː) stay in the cell of the plain sound.

### Vowels

| | Front | Back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Close** | i iː ḭ | u uː ṵ |
| **Close-mid** | e |  |
| **Open-mid** | ɛ ɛ̰ | ɔ ɔː |
| **Open** | a aː a̰ |  |

Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: long vowels iː uː aː ɔː. Nasality: no nasal vowels. Phonation: ḭ ṵ ɛ̰ a̰.

### Tone, syllables and stress

No phonemic tone.
Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 33%, CVC 29%, CCV 13%, CCVC 10%, CVCC 6%, V 4%, VC 3%, CCVCC 2%. At most 2 consonant(s) before the vowel and 2 after it.
Stress falls on the first syllable. The IPA on this page marks it with ˈ before the stressed syllable.
Core words average 1.47 syllables (3.6 sounds); 30% of words share their form with another word.

### Allophony

This output records no allophones (the engine stores sounds as phonemes only).

### Phonological rules

Rules the language applies today, in order. A new sound change starts as a rule applying across words; as it ages it narrows to words, then to word-making, and in the end dies, leaving its alternations in single words.

| # | rule | applies | since | example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | i → j, u → w / _V (glide formation) | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~5 kyr ago | i- + ɔ → jɔ 'agent-day (not night)' |
| 2 | b → ∅, c → ∅, d → ∅, dʒ → ∅ / C_# (final cluster simplification: the last of two final consonants lost) | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~3.5 kyr ago | – |
| 3 | a → ɛ / [+stress] open syllable | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2.5 kyr ago | aw + -ɛ → ɛwɛ 'egg-intens' |
| 4 | j → ∅ / V_V | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2 kyr ago | i- + juh → iuh 'agent-fly (insect)' |
| 5 | l → w / _C, _# | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2 kyr ago | – |
| 6 | l → r / lX*_ (the second of two l's in a word becomes r) | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | bliː + lɔ → bliːrɔ 'be alive + bone (compound)' |
| 7 | a → ∅, aː → ∅, a̰ → ∅, e → ∅ / C_# [−stress] | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | pep + -ɛ → pep 'arm or hand-intens' |
| 8 | r → l / _X*r (the first of two r's in a word becomes l) | across words in a phrase and inside words | ~0.5 kyr ago | – |

Lately dead: S019 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S199 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); assimilation.nasal_place (old: its alternations are now learned word by word, 0 kyr ago); S039 (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago); S122/ṵ (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago); reduction.syncope (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago).

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · n ‹n› · ɲ ‹ny› · p ‹p› · b ‹b› · t ‹t› · d ‹d› · c ‹ky› · k ‹k› · ɡ ‹g› · ʔ ‹'› · dʒ ‹j› · s̪ ‹s̮› ‹s› · s ‹s› · ʃ ‹sh› · f ‹f› · h ‹h› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l ‹l› · r ‹rr›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · ḭ ‹ḭ› ‹i› · iː ‹ii› · u ‹u› · ṵ ‹ṵ› ‹u› · uː ‹uu› · e ‹e› · ɛ ‹è› ‹e› · ɛ̰ ‹ḛ̀› ‹e› · ɔ ‹o› · ɔː ‹oo› · a ‹a› · a̰ ‹a̰› ‹a› · aː ‹aa›

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SVO; it has prepositions. In the noun phrase: possessed before the possessor; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; numeral before the noun; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has a definite article after the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), no grammatical number, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark perfective, progressive and habitual; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a verb form. Verbs agree with the subject by prefixes; not with the object.
Other features: alienable and inalienable possession told apart; a copula; a bound causative; no passive; question words moved to the front; a decimal counting base; locational possession ('at me is a dog').
Measured morphology: 12 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.7 (0 free word … 3 fused), 28 paradigm cells, 13 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (pinu), 'at' (klɔ), 'with' (naːb) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** There is no gender or noun class.

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Perfect (PRF): a separate word before the verb (naːb, from 'hold'); progressive (PROG): a clitic before the verb (ɡwe, from 'at'); habitual (HAB): a clitic before the verb (i, from 'know'). Unmarked: past, future (left to context).

| *naːb* | *du* |
| --- | --- |
| PRF | go |

‘(it) has gone’

| *ɡwe=du* |
| --- |
| PROG=go |

‘(it) is going’

| *i=du* |
| --- |
| HAB=go |

‘(it) usually goes’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 1SG: a prefix (u, from 'I'); 2SG: a prefix (i, from 'thou'); 3PL: a prefix (ɛ, from 'they'). No marker yet for 3SG, 1PL, 2PL (zero).

| *u-t* |
| --- |
| 1SG-go |

‘I go’

| *i-d* |
| --- |
| 2SG-go |

‘you go’

| *ɛ-d* |
| --- |
| 3PL-go |

‘they go’

**Negation.** Negation uses the word for 'not' (pɛ), preverbal.

| *u* | *pɛ* | *u-wi* | *ʃijʃibɲ-naw* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | NEG | 1SG-drink | milk-DEF |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a marker on the verb. Question words move to the front: who ɛ, what ɡwe, where nɛw, when nɛ, how ɡwew.

| *i* | *mɛ=ji-baw* | *mɛbmap-naw* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | Q=2SG-hear | thunder-DEF |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *ɡwe* | *bap-naw* | *iɛ̰* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what | child-DEF | bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *umṵb* | *ʃin-naw* |
| --- | --- |
| eat | fish-DEF |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands after the possessed noun, with no marker. Kin and body parts (inalienable) take no genitive marker. 'Having' is said with a locational phrase ('at my mother is a boat').

| *huː* | *uj-naw* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | man-DEF |

‘the man's dog’

| *klɔ* | *nɛn* | *u* | *bi-mɛɡṵwʃij* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| at | mother | 1SG | COP-boat |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *bak-naw* | *naw* | *uːɔw* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| woman-DEF | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a prefix (bi, from 'he').

| *naw* | *uj* | *bi-jic* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| that | man | COP-merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *ʃij-naw* | *bi-cɔːraj* |
| --- | --- |
| water-DEF | COP-cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Giving (two objects).** Double object: theme and recipient both unmarked.

| *bak-naw* | *ɡwjɛ̰w* | *ʃin* | *bap-naw* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| woman-DEF | give | fish | child-DEF |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is unnṵp and a hundred is kuf.

| *ibaf* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *mɛp* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *bɛh* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *uj-naw* | *elij* | *huː-naw* | *mwe* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man-DEF | say | dog-DEF | sleep |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 13 below)

**Word shapes.** Some markers sound the same: 2SG and HAB are both i (context tells them apart).

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' ɲipɲip (near) and 'that' naw (far).

| *ɲipɲip* | *huː* |
| --- | --- |
| this | dog |

‘this dog’

| *naw* | *huː* |
| --- | --- |
| that | dog |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** A locational comparison: the standard takes the word for 'at' ('big at B'), as Swahili kuliko 'where there is'.

| *uj-naw* | *bi-nɛmaw* | *klɔ* | *huː-naw* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man-DEF | COP-big | at | dog-DEF |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 14 below)

Counting base: decimal. Several numerals began as other words: two < 'pair'; eight = 'four + two'; nine = 'ten + one'; ten = 'hand two'; twenty = 'ten two'.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are one meaningful word; the byname is the father's name in the genitive with 'son' or 'daughter'. The tradition goes back to the hobgoblin proto-language.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **O** | /ɔ/ | 'sun' | old | O 'sun': o 'sun'; an old name, coined in d478 4.0 kyr ago as O |
| **Meyrray** | /mɛjraj/ | 'snow' | old | Meyrray 'snow': meyrray 'snow'; an old name, coined in d478 4.0 kyr ago as Meyrray |
| **Berray** | /bɛraj/ | 'dove' | old | Berray 'dove': berray 'dove'; an old name, coined in d478 4.0 kyr ago as Berray |
| **Guwyiy** | /ɡṵwjḭj/ | 'rain' | new | Guwyiy 'rain': gwyiy 'rain'; coined from today's words |
| **Bi** | /bi/ | 'flower' | new | Bi 'flower': bi 'flower'; coined from today's words |
| **Hemaf** | /hɛmaf/ | 'fire' | new | Hemaf 'fire': hamaf 'fire'; coined from today's words |
| **O Me'kyuymeyrray** | /ɔ mɛʔcujmɛjraj/ | 'sun, son of snow' | patronymic | the father's name Meyrray + me'kyuy 'son' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |
| **Meyrray Hofberray** | /mɛjraj hɔfbɛraj/ | 'snow, daughter of dove' | patronymic | the father's name Berray + hof 'daughter' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |

**Settlements.** **Erreb** /ɛreb/ (village, 721): 'the good field'; fence + the old name: 'fence good field' (a tautology, like River Avon); named by the human (d561) who founded it 4.7 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Owenin** /ɔwenin/ (village, 551): 'Infa's house'; named by the human (d561.1) who founded it 0.5 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Ewubyoh** /ɛwubjɔh/ (village, 504): 'Ohio's village'; named by the human (d561.1) who founded it 0.5 kyr ago, kept as heard.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
